name: Nephrotic syndrome

matching.reasoningTemplate: Heavy proteinuria with oedema and hypoalbuminaemia defines the nephrotic syndrome.

redFlags: Thrombosis & infection risk; consider underlying cause

harrison.pages: Harrison 22e: p.324 (edema in nephrotic syndrome), p.384-385 (proteinuria & vascular causes, Ch.55), p.2356-2359 (proteinuric states & nephrotic syndrome, Ch.319)
clinicalPearls: Heavy proteinuria (>3.5 g/d) can occur WITHOUT the full nephrotic picture (no hypoalbuminaemia/oedema/hyperlipidaemia) in several renal diseases, notably diabetes; proteinuria is not synonymous with nephrotic syndrome (p.385, p.2357).

Periorbital, facial and eyelid swelling (worst on waking) helps distinguish nephrotic oedema from the dependent oedema/orthopnoea of heart failure; penile and scrotal oedema may be severe enough to obstruct urinary flow in men (p.324, p.2358).
Severe oedema can produce skin bullae that rupture and predispose to ulceration and cellulitis; vocal cord oedema may cause hoarseness (p.2358).
Urine microscopy may show oval fat bodies (lipid-laden tubular epithelial cells), cholesterol monohydrate Maltese-cross crystals under polarised light, and fatty casts (p.2358).
Rapid-onset hypoalbuminaemia may produce horizontal white nail-bed lines (Muehrcke's lines) (p.2358).

Abrupt adult-onset nephrotic syndrome with markedly elevated cholesterol suggests a podocytopathy such as minimal change disease, which is often preceded by upper respiratory infection, allergy or immunisation (p.2358).

Dipstick detects predominantly albumin and the most acidic proteins; it misses kappa/lambda light chains (myeloma), so a normal dipstick does not exclude overflow proteinuria — send urine protein electrophoresis/immunoelectrophoresis (p.385, p.2357).

Nephrotic-range proteinuria without oedema, with rapid renal function loss, raises HIV-associated nephropathy (collapsing glomerulopathy, a severe treatment-resistant FSGS variant), more common in patients of African ancestry (p.2358).
harrison.pathophysiology: Nephrotic syndrome reflects increased glomerular permeability to plasma proteins. Minimal change disease causes diffuse fusion (effacement) of podocyte foot processes producing predominantly 'selective' albumin loss, whereas immune-complex disruption of the basement membrane and slit diaphragms yields 'nonselective' loss of albumin and larger proteins. Hypoalbuminaemia results from urinary loss plus increased proximal-tubule catabolism of filtered albumin, exceeding hepatic synthesis (a hypercatabolic, negative-nitrogen-balance state). Oedema arises from renal sodium retention and reduced plasma oncotic pressure; perceived reduction in effective intravascular volume activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, AVP and the sympathetic nervous system, and filtered proteases can directly activate the epithelial Na channel (ENaC) in principal cells, promoting further salt/water retention. Hyperlipidaemia/hypercholesterolaemia reflect increased hepatic lipoprotein synthesis. Notably, hypertension is uncommon in primary kidney diseases causing nephrotic syndrome (p.385). Hereditary nephrotic syndrome can result from podocyte slit-diaphragm gene mutations (nephrin NPHS1, podocin NPHS2); APOL1 risk variants predispose to FSGS, with disease expression triggered by a 'second hit' of infection/inflammation damaging podocytes and glomerular endothelium (p.2357-2358).
additionalDifferentials: Minimal change disease (idiopathic; secondary to Hodgkin's lymphoma or other lymphoproliferative disorders) — predominant cause in children <6 years (p.2358)

Primary FSGS / podocytopathy versus secondary FSGS (remnant kidney after partial nephrectomy, adaptive injury, chronic hypoxaemia, sickle cell disease, obesity, heroin, congenital urogenital anomalies) (p.2358)

Membranous nephropathy — ~70% of primary cases associated with anti-PLA2R antibodies; secondary forms with malignancy (GI, prostate, breast, lung, bladder), SLE, drugs (gold, penicillamine, NSAIDs), infections (p.2358 Fig.319-3)
Membranoproliferative / C3 glomerulopathy and dense-deposit disease (hypocomplementaemia); secondary to SLE, cryoglobulins, SBE (p.2358 Fig.319-3)
Diabetic glomerulosclerosis (subnephrotic albuminuria progressing to nephrotic range) (p.324, p.2356)
Amyloidosis (AL light-chain, AA/SAA from chronic inflammation) (p.2358 Fig.319-3)
Multiple myeloma / plasma cell dyscrasia with light-chain (overflow) proteinuria not detected by dipstick (p.385, p.2357)
infectionMimics: Postinfectious glomerulonephritis and COVID-19-associated glomerular injury (p.2358 Fig.319-3)

Quartan malarial nephropathy — chronic Plasmodium malariae immune-complex injury causing focal/segmental glomerulonephritis with capillary basement-membrane splitting, mainly in children, responds poorly to therapy (p.~1670 malaria chapter)
nonInfectiousMimics: Heart failure oedema — dependent with orthopnoea, contrasts with periorbital/facial nephrotic oedema (p.324, p.2358)
Hepatic cirrhosis with hypoalbuminaemia and oedema/ascites (p.325)
Severe malnutrition and protein-losing enteropathy as alternative hypoalbuminaemic states (p.324)
additionalInvestigations: Spot morning urine albumin-to-creatinine or protein-to-creatinine ratio (normalised to creatinine to discount urine dilution) or 24-h urine protein/albumin — preferred over dipstick for quantification (p.385, p.2357)
Serum and urine protein immunoelectrophoresis / UPEP to detect light chains when myeloma is possible (dipstick misses light chains) (p.385, p.2357)
Urine microscopy for oval fat bodies, Maltese-cross lipid crystals and fatty casts (p.2358)
Anti-PLA2R antibody testing in suspected primary membranous nephropathy (p.2358)
Imaging/angiography for suspected renal vein thrombosis presenting with heavy proteinuria and haematuria (p.384)
redFlags: Heavy proteinuria with new haematuria suggesting renal vein thrombosis (p.384)
Rapidly declining renal function with very heavy proteinuria and no oedema suggesting collapsing glomerulopathy/HIVAN (p.2358)
Cellulitis or ulceration from ruptured oedema bullae (p.2358)
Hoarseness from vocal cord oedema or scrotal/penile oedema obstructing urinary flow (p.2358)
harrison.prognosis: Glomerular proteinuria in diabetes typically appears after years of small-vessel disease (hence frequent coexistent retinopathy) and predicts progression to nephrotic syndrome and renal failure; the rate of progression is faster with hypertension, obesity and poor glucose control. Diffuse glomerular involvement (most glomeruli) makes nephrotic syndrome likely, whereas focal disease (<50% of glomeruli) tends to give subnephrotic albuminuria. In membranous nephropathy, ~70% of primary cases are anti-PLA2R associated. Collapsing glomerulopathy (HIVAN) is a severe, treatment-resistant FSGS variant. Quartan malarial nephropathy responds poorly to therapy (p.2356-2358).
pitfalls: Assuming any nephrotic-range proteinuria equals classic nephrotic syndrome — heavy proteinuria can occur without hypoalbuminaemia/oedema (p.385).
Relying on dipstick alone — it misses light chains, so myeloma-associated overflow proteinuria can be overlooked; total protein:creatinine ratio is not specific for albumin (p.385, p.2357).
Equating subnephrotic albuminuria with absence of significant glomerular disease — focal disease causes lower albuminuria yet can be significant (p.2357).
Misreading biopsy-proven FSGS as a single entity — primary podocytopathic FSGS, secondary/adaptive FSGS, and post-GN healing scars are distinct (p.2356, p.2398).
harrison.severityClassification: Albuminuria categories (Ch.55 Fig.55-3): moderately increased 30-300 mg/d or mg/g (formerly microalbuminuria); severely increased 300-3500 mg/d or mg/g (formerly macroalbuminuria); nephrotic range >3500 mg/d or mg/g. Full nephrotic syndrome defined by the triad of oedema, hypoalbuminaemia (<3.5 g/dL) and proteinuria >3.5 g/d, usually with lipid abnormalities (high LDL, low HDL, lipiduria) (p.385, p.2357).
